questions.stem: Which types of mental health problems are the most prevalent among adolescents?
options: personality disorders and psychosis
eating disorders and phobias of heights
dementia and other memory disorders
anxiety disorders and depression
questions.explanation: Anxiety disorders and depression are the most common mental health problems among young people. Early, effective treatment is important because many adult disorders begin in adolescence.

questions.stem: Which description best distinguishes an anxiety disorder from everyday anxiety?
options: The anxiety causes a faster heart rate and sweaty palms
The anxiety passes once the stressful situation is over
It is excessive, lasting and interferes with daily life
The anxiety occurs before an important event such as an exam
questions.explanation: Everyday anxiety is a normal, short-lived response to a stressor. An anxiety disorder involves fear or worry out of proportion to the situation that lasts and disrupts study, work or relationships.

questions.stem: Cognitive-behavioural therapy is based on the idea that:
options: mental illness is caused only by chemical imbalances, which must be corrected with medication
unconscious childhood conflicts must be uncovered before any symptoms can improve
people should be left to find their own solutions without any guidance from a therapist
thoughts, feelings and behaviours are linked, so changing thoughts and actions eases distress
questions.explanation: CBT holds that unhelpful thinking patterns and behaviours maintain distress. By identifying and changing them, the person's emotions also change. It is structured and present-focused rather than exploring the unconscious.

questions.stem: A student with depression thinks 'I failed one test, so I am useless at everything'. In CBT, the therapist helps her test the evidence for this thought and replace it with a more balanced one. This technique is called:
options: behavioural activation
response cost
cognitive restructuring
systematic desensitisation
questions.explanation: Cognitive restructuring involves identifying unhelpful automatic thoughts, examining the evidence and replacing them with more realistic ones. Behavioural activation instead targets what the person does.

questions.stem: A man with depression has stopped seeing friends and spends most days in bed. His psychologist helps him schedule small, enjoyable activities each day. Which part of CBT is this?
options: cognitive restructuring
flooding
a fear hierarchy
behavioural activation
questions.explanation: Depression is maintained by withdrawal, which reduces opportunities for reward. Behavioural activation gradually reintroduces rewarding activities to lift mood. A fear hierarchy is used for anxiety and phobias.

questions.stem: A teenager with social anxiety believes 'Everyone will laugh at me if I speak in class'. Which CBT plan best targets both the thought and the behaviour?
options: Challenge the prediction, then test it by speaking briefly in class
Avoid speaking in class until the belief disappears without help
Take medication only, so the thought no longer needs to be examined
Explore early memories to find the unconscious cause of the fear
questions.explanation: CBT combines cognitive work, such as questioning the evidence for the prediction, with behavioural experiments that test it in real life. Avoidance keeps anxiety going because the belief is never disproved.

questions.stem: Why do CBT therapists often set homework between sessions?
options: Practising skills in daily life helps the changes generalise and last
Homework replaces the need for any further sessions with the therapist
Homework allows the therapist to diagnose the client's disorder
Homework is used to punish clients who miss their appointments
questions.explanation: CBT is skills-based, so practising thought records or graded tasks in real situations helps clients apply what they learn. This supports lasting change after therapy ends.

questions.stem: Which statement about CBT for anxiety and depression is best supported?
options: It helps many people, but needs active effort and suits some better than others
It works equally well for every person regardless of age, culture or motivation
It cures depression permanently after a single session for most people
It is effective only when combined with electroconvulsive therapy
questions.explanation: CBT has strong research support for anxiety and depression, but it demands effort and engagement, and some people need it adapted or combined with other treatments. No treatment works equally for everyone.

questions.stem: George Engel proposed that a biopsychosocial model be adopted when patients present for treatment. Which treatment plan for depression best reflects this model?
options: medication review, CBT and help to reconnect with family and friends
CBT sessions alone, focusing only on the client's negative thoughts
medication alone, adjusted until the client's depressive symptoms decrease
advice to rest at home and avoid all social contact for a month
questions.explanation: The biopsychosocial model addresses biological factors, such as medication or sleep, psychological factors, such as thinking patterns, and social factors, such as support and relationships, together.

questions.stem: Which thought is most typical of the cognitive pattern that CBT targets in depression?
options: Nothing ever goes right for me
I did badly on this task, so I will practise more
Some days are harder than others for most people
I can ask a friend for help with this problem
questions.explanation: Depression is associated with negative, overgeneralised thoughts about the self, the world and the future. CBT helps clients notice such thoughts and test whether they are accurate. The other thoughts are balanced and adaptive.

questions.stem: In CBT, an automatic thought is:
options: a deliberate plan written down during a therapy session
a quick, often unnoticed thought that pops up in response to a situation
a reflex such as blinking that is controlled by the spinal cord
a memory of a childhood conflict that has been repressed
questions.explanation: Automatic thoughts arise rapidly and are often accepted without question. In anxiety and depression they are frequently negative or distorted, so CBT teaches clients to notice and evaluate them.

questions.stem: Why is avoidance a problem in anxiety disorders and phobias?
options: It replaces anxious thoughts with balanced ones without any effort
It brings short-term relief, which negatively reinforces avoiding the fear
It increases exposure to the feared object, which strengthens the fear
It causes the person to learn relaxation in the presence of the fear
questions.explanation: Escaping or avoiding the feared situation reduces anxiety in the short term, so avoidance is negatively reinforced. The person never learns that the situation is safe, so the fear persists.

questions.stem: Systematic desensitisation is mainly used to treat:
options: specific phobias
major depression
personality disorders
sleep deprivation
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitisation gradually reduces an intense, irrational fear of a particular object or situation by pairing it with relaxation. It is a standard treatment for specific phobias.

questions.stem: What are the three main steps of systematic desensitisation, in order?
options: gradual exposure, then learn relaxation, then build a fear hierarchy
learn relaxation, face the worst fear first, then build a fear hierarchy
learn relaxation, build a fear hierarchy, then gradual exposure while relaxed
build a fear hierarchy, face the worst fear first, then learn to relax deeply
questions.explanation: The client first learns a relaxation technique, then ranks feared situations from least to most anxiety-provoking. They then work up the hierarchy while relaxed, moving on only when the current step causes little anxiety.

questions.stem: A woman with a phobia of dogs builds a fear hierarchy. Which item should be placed at the bottom?
options: watching a video of a dog barking
looking at a cartoon drawing of a dog
patting a large, friendly dog on its head
standing next to a dog on a lead
questions.explanation: The bottom of the hierarchy is the least anxiety-provoking situation, such as a cartoon. Patting a dog would be at or near the top.

questions.stem: During systematic desensitisation, a client becomes very anxious at step 5 of 10. What should the therapist do?
options: skip to step 10 so the client confronts the fear all at once
end the treatment, because anxiety shows the method has failed
punish the anxious response so the client stops showing it
go back a step and re-establish relaxation before moving on
questions.explanation: The method relies on the client staying relaxed at each step. If anxiety becomes high, going back to a step they can manage keeps the feared stimulus paired with relaxation rather than fear.

questions.stem: Why might a therapist choose systematic desensitisation rather than flooding for a child with a phobia of needles?
options: It is the only treatment for phobias that is based on conditioning
It is gradual and less distressing, so the child is likelier to finish
It works faster, because the most feared item is faced in the first session
It does not require the child to experience the feared stimulus at all
questions.explanation: Flooding exposes the person to the most feared stimulus immediately, which can be very distressing and may lead to dropout. Systematic desensitisation is gradual and gives the client more control. Both involve exposure to the feared stimulus.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of systematic desensitisation?
options: It works only for phobias that began in early childhood
It can be slow and depends on the client relaxing and facing the fear
It cannot be used for any phobia that involves an animal or an insect
It requires the client to take anti-anxiety medication throughout treatment
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitisation is effective for many specific phobias, but it can be slow and some clients find it hard to relax or to imagine scenes vividly. It does not require medication.

questions.stem: Before beginning treatment for a phobia, a psychologist explains the process, possible discomfort and the client's right to stop. This addresses which ethical requirement?
options: debriefing
deception
informed consent
confidentiality
questions.explanation: Informed consent requires that the client understands what treatment involves, including any discomfort and risks, and agrees voluntarily. Clients may withdraw from treatment at any time.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old is being treated for depression. What ethical issue must the psychologist consider about confidentiality?
options: It never applies to any clients who are under 18 years of age
It means information must be shared with the client's school
It allows details to be posted online if names are removed
It may be limited if there is a serious risk of harm to anyone
questions.explanation: Confidentiality is central to treatment, but psychologists must explain its limits, such as when there is a serious risk to the client's safety. Information is not shared with schools or others without consent.

questions.stem: Exposure-based treatments for phobias deliberately cause some anxiety. Why can they still be considered ethical?
options: Clients are not allowed to stop once the treatment has properly started
Anxiety caused during treatment does not count as psychological harm
Therapists are not required to explain the procedure beforehand
The discomfort is brief, explained beforehand and outweighed by benefits
questions.explanation: Ethical practice weighs short-term discomfort against long-term benefit. The client must give informed consent, be able to stop and be supported throughout.

questions.stem: Which situation would be an ethical concern in treating anxiety?
options: a psychologist using a treatment with research support
a psychologist treating a close friend as a client
a psychologist referring a client to a specialist
a psychologist explaining the limits of confidentiality
questions.explanation: Treating a friend creates a dual relationship, which can compromise objectivity and the client's welfare. Referring on, explaining confidentiality and using evidence-based treatment are good practice.

questions.stem: A psychologist wants to use a new, untested technique on clients with depression without telling them it is experimental. What is the main ethical problem?
options: Depression must be treated only with medication by law
Clients with depression are not able to make any decisions
Clients cannot give informed consent to a treatment that is hidden
New techniques must never be developed or tested in clinical psychology
questions.explanation: Clients have a right to know the nature, risks and evidence for a treatment before agreeing to it. Hiding that a technique is experimental removes their ability to make an informed choice.

questions.stem: In psychology, resilience refers to:
options: the ability to recover quickly from setbacks and adapt
the complete absence of stress or difficulties in a person's life
a fixed trait that some people are born with and others never have
the tendency to avoid difficult situations so they never cause harm
questions.explanation: Resilience is the capacity to cope with and bounce back from adversity. Resilient people still experience stress, and resilience can be developed over time.

questions.stem: Which is an internal factor of resilience?
options: a caring, encouraging teacher
a safe neighbourhood
an optimistic outlook
a supportive extended family
questions.explanation: Internal factors lie within the person, such as optimism, self-esteem, problem-solving skills and emotional regulation. Family, teachers and neighbourhoods are external factors.

questions.stem: Which is an external factor of resilience?
options: an internal locus of control
the ability to manage emotions
strong connections with a sporting club
good problem-solving skills and planning
questions.explanation: External factors come from a person's environment and relationships, such as community groups, friends and family. The other options are personal qualities and so are internal factors.

questions.stem: Two students both fail an important exam. One blames herself as stupid and gives up; the other decides she needs a better study plan and asks her teacher for help. Which protective factors does the second student show?
options: a pessimistic explanatory style and reliance on luck to improve
high stress and a belief that intelligence cannot change
an internal locus of control and realistic planning
an external locus of control and a tendency to avoid difficulties
questions.explanation: Believing outcomes are within her control and making a realistic plan help her recover from the setback. These are internal protective factors linked to resilience.

questions.stem: Why is having an internal locus of control considered a protective factor?
options: People believe their own actions can change outcomes
People believe outcomes depend on luck, so they do not worry about them
People blame others for problems, which protects their self-esteem
People avoid challenges, so they experience fewer setbacks
questions.explanation: An internal locus of control is the belief that one's own effort and choices influence what happens. This encourages problem-solving and persistence after setbacks.

questions.stem: Being a good communicator is linked to resilience mainly because it helps a person:
options: seek support and resolve problems with others
avoid having to rely on anyone else at all
hide their feelings so others are not burdened
win arguments by talking over other people
questions.explanation: Good communication helps people express needs, ask for help and resolve conflict, which builds and draws on social support, an important protective factor.

questions.stem: A young person has strong internal resilience factors but moves to a new town where they know no one. Which statement best describes their risk?
options: Internal factors alone guarantee they will cope well with any adversity
External factors only matter for children, so the move will not affect them
Resilience is fixed, so moving to a new town cannot change it
Losing external supports may reduce resilience until new connections form
questions.explanation: Resilience depends on both internal and external factors, which interact. Losing friends and community removes supports, so building new connections is important.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of a strategy a person could use to become more resilient?
options: noticing and challenging catastrophic thoughts after a setback
avoiding any situation where failure might be possible
relying on others to solve every problem as it arises
suppressing all negative emotions so they are not felt
questions.explanation: Resilience skills can be learned, such as realistic thinking, problem-solving, emotional regulation and building social connections. Avoidance and suppression tend to reduce coping in the long term.

questions.stem: The Penn Resilience Program teaches students to recognise how their beliefs about events affect their feelings and to challenge unrealistic beliefs. Which approach is it based on?
options: systematic desensitisation
cognitive-behavioural principles
psychodynamic principles
behaviour modification with tokens
questions.explanation: The program applies cognitive-behavioural ideas, such as the link between beliefs and emotional consequences, to build skills for coping with stress. It is delivered in groups, often through schools.

questions.stem: A school wants to evaluate whether a resilience program reduces depressive symptoms. Which design gives the strongest evidence?
options: interview teachers about whether students seem happier this year
randomly assign classes to the program or a control, then compare
survey students who chose the program about whether they enjoyed it
measure symptoms only after the program in the students who took part
questions.explanation: Random allocation and a control group allow differences to be attributed to the program, and measuring over time shows whether effects last. Satisfaction surveys and post-only measures cannot show the program caused change.

questions.stem: Resilience training is used as a psychological intervention mainly to:
options: replace treatment for people with severe mental illness
remove all sources of stress from a person's life
help people cope with stress before it becomes illness
diagnose mental disorders in people who have no symptoms
questions.explanation: Resilience programs are preventive: they build coping skills so that stress is less likely to develop into problems such as depression. They do not replace treatment for existing severe illness.

questions.stem: Barbara Fredrickson's broaden-and-build theory links positive emotions to resilience. Which statement reflects the theory?
options: Positive emotions are useful only when there is no stress present
Positive emotions must be suppressed so that problems can be solved
Positive emotions broaden thinking and build lasting personal resources
Positive emotions narrow attention so people focus on immediate threats
questions.explanation: The theory proposes that positive emotions widen the range of thoughts and actions people consider, which over time builds resources such as social bonds and coping skills. Negative emotions, by contrast, narrow attention.

questions.stem: Holding positive views of oneself and one's abilities supports resilience because it:
options: makes a person unaware of the risks in difficult situations
means a person no longer needs support from other people
builds confidence to tackle problems and keep going
removes any chance that a person will experience failure
questions.explanation: Positive self-regard and self-efficacy encourage people to keep trying and to see setbacks as manageable. They do not prevent failure or remove the value of social support.
